Manchester's Housing Loan Controversy

£983 million in cumulative housing loans, a tiny affordable-homes share, and serious questions about who regeneration has served.

By Steve English · 8 October 2026

Manchester's post-industrial rebirth has been sold as a success story. But the public evidence raises a harder question: after vast public-backed investment, how much affordable housing did ordinary Mancunians actually receive?

A recent report by the World Socialist Web Site drew attention to the Greater Manchester Housing Investment Fund (GMHIF), its loans to private developers and Manchester's wider relationship with Abu Dhabi-linked investment. Its political interpretation is its own. The underlying documents, however, deserve a much wider audience.

The figures that demand answers

  • Cumulative GMHIF lending was reported as £983 million by 2024.
  • An evaluation reported 679 affordable homes from 10,974 homes delivered or forecast through the fund — about 6.2%.
  • Developer Renaker was reported as receiving more than £500 million in loans.

Public risk, private development

There is nothing inherently improper about a public body lending for regeneration. The question is whether the public gets a fair return: genuinely affordable homes, clear safeguards, repayment, and transparency about who benefits.

The fund's evaluation shows a striking mismatch between the scale of public finance and the affordable-housing outcome. Six per cent is not evidence that the scheme delivered nothing; it is evidence that the affordable element was small beside the total number of homes it supported.

For a city in a housing crisis, that ought to be the centre of the debate. Towers may transform a skyline, but a regeneration strategy should be judged by whether people on ordinary local incomes can live in the city it creates.

Land, influence and transparency

Research by the University of Sheffield examined land and development relationships involving Manchester, Abu Dhabi-linked investors and Manchester City. It raised questions about the terms on which strategically valuable public land was made available and whether the public interest had been adequately protected.

That is not the same as proving wrongdoing. Nor is it a basis for casually assigning every Manchester Council decision to Andy Burnham. Manchester City Council, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and the mayoralty are distinct institutions with different legal powers and decision-makers.

But Burnham has been the elected Mayor of Greater Manchester since 2017 and has made the city's development model a central part of his political identity. He cannot plausibly claim that the outcomes of a major combined-authority housing fund are beneath public scrutiny.

The test is simple: What affordable-housing requirements were attached to each major loan; how were they enforced; what was the public return; and why did the overall affordable share end up so low?

What needs to be published

Greater Manchester should publish a plain-English, scheme-by-scheme account of all GMHIF loans: the borrower, amount, interest and security, homes delivered, affordable homes delivered, any changes to terms, and repayments received. The public should not have to stitch this together from evaluations, planning documents and investigative reporting.

Burnham should also set out his own role: what he approved, what he inherited, what levers he had, and what he will change. If the model is as successful as its champions claim, that transparency would strengthen the case. If it is not, Manchester residents deserve to know before the next billion is committed.

Sources and further reading

  • World Socialist Web Site: “Manchester City financial scandal rocks Burnham government” — the article that prompted this investigation; claims should be assessed against the primary material below.
  • Greater Manchester Combined Authority: Greater Manchester Housing Investment Fund.
